lesson.title: Left and Right: The Two Halves of a Derivative
lesson.summary: A one-sided derivative measures the instantaneous rate of change as you approach a point from only the left or only the right, and full differentiability requires both sides to agree.
lesson.body:
The ordinary derivative f'(a) is defined by a two-sided limit: you let h approach 0 through both positive and negative values and ask whether the difference quotient settles on a single number. But just as a two-sided limit can be broken into a left-hand limit and a right-hand limit, the derivative can be broken into a left-hand derivative and a right-hand derivative. The right-hand derivative is f'_+(a) = lim as h approaches 0 from the positive side of [f(a+h) - f(a)] / h, and the left-hand derivative is f'_-(a) = lim as h approaches 0 from the negative side of that same quotient. Each one asks the same question as the ordinary derivative, but restricts the approach to only one direction.

This is exactly the same logic used for one-sided limits: a two-sided limit exists precisely when the left-hand and right-hand limits both exist and are equal. The derivative obeys the identical rule at the level of the difference quotient. A function is differentiable at a point a if and only if f'_-(a) and f'_+(a) both exist as finite numbers and are equal to each other, in which case f'(a) is that common value. If the two one-sided derivatives disagree, or if either one fails to exist, the two-sided derivative does not exist at that point, even if the function is perfectly continuous there.

Consider f(x) = |x| at a = 0, a case where continuity clearly holds but differentiability is in question. For h > 0, |0+h| - |0| over h equals h/h = 1, so f'_+(0) = 1. For h < 0, |h| = -h, so the quotient is -h/h = -1, giving f'_-(0) = -1. Since 1 does not equal -1, the two one-sided derivatives disagree, and f is not differentiable at 0, even though it is continuous there. Geometrically, the graph approaches the origin along a line of slope -1 from the left and departs along a line of slope 1 from the right, producing a sharp corner rather than a single well-defined tangent line.

Not every piecewise function behaves this badly. Let g(x) = x^2 for x less than or equal to 1, and g(x) = 2x - 1 for x greater than 1. First check continuity at x = 1: the left piece gives 1^2 = 1, and the right piece gives 2(1) - 1 = 1, so the two pieces meet up and g is continuous there. Now check the one-sided derivatives. The left piece has derivative 2x, so g'_-(1) = 2(1) = 2. The right piece has derivative 2, a constant, so g'_+(1) = 2 as well. The one-sided derivatives agree, so g is differentiable at x = 1 with g'(1) = 2, even though g is defined by two different formulas on either side.

One-sided derivatives matter beyond textbook curiosities. Engineers designing splines or cams need curves whose pieces match not just in value but in slope, which is precisely a check that the one-sided derivatives agree at each seam. Physicists modeling a process that changes rule at some threshold, such as a spring that only resists compression past a certain point, use one-sided derivatives to describe the rate of change right up to and away from that threshold. In every case, the underlying idea is the same one used for one-sided limits: restrict the direction of approach, then compare what you get from each side.
